transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Hi. Yeah, thank you. Um, so, honestly, it's just been a lot lately, and I guess that's what made me finally come in. I just... I keep having these overwhelming feelings that I've completely ruined things for everybody around me. 

I'm in an apprenticeship right now—I'm a pipefitter and plumber—and I got my associate's degree before this, so my parents and everyone made this really huge deal about me getting into the trades and getting a good union spot. But lately, I just feel like a complete and total fake. Like I'm totally tricking the journeymen into thinking I know what I'm doing, when I don't. And it's just this incredibly heavy feeling, you know? I look at my family, who brag about me all the time to their friends, and I just feel like I'm letting them down so badly by being an imposter. And even at work, there are these younger apprentices who just started their first year, and they kind of look to me to know what's going on because I've been there a little longer, and I just feel like I'm failing them too. I'm supposed to be setting a good example and I'm just not.

And the most frustrating part is that I'm feeling this way over stuff that really shouldn't be a big deal. Like, minor mistakes on a job site. I know for a fact that if anyone else on the crew made the same mistake—like mismeasuring something by a fraction of an inch or taking a little too long to thread a pipe—they would just fix it, grab a new piece of material, and move right on with their day like nothing happened. It's just part of the job. But for me, I just dwell on it. I can't let it go. I feel like this massive burden on the whole crew, like I'm dragging the entire project down and ruining the day because I'm a fraud. I just can't seem to shake this awful guilt that I'm messing everything up for everyone.
Do you feel like a fraud or imposter in areas of your life outside of work, like with friends, family, or in school?

Um, no, actually. It’s... it's really just work, which I guess is kind of weird? Like, when I was in school getting my associate's, I never felt like this at all. School just made sense to me. I was the person who would sit in the library for, like, three or four hours straight with all my different colored highlighters, making sure every single note was perfectly organized. I knew exactly what the professors wanted, I knew how to study for the tests, so I never felt like an imposter there. I felt like I totally earned my grades and my degree. 

And with my friends... no, definitely not. I've known most of my core group since high school, so they know exactly who I am, you know? The good and the bad. We still hang out at all the same places, like this one diner downtown we always go to on Friday nights—we always try to get the same booth in the back—and I don't have to put on a show for them. I can just talk about whatever, and I don't feel like I'm tricking them into liking me or anything. They just know me. 

Even with my parents... I mean, like I was saying, I feel incredibly guilty that they think I'm doing so great at work when I feel like I'm completely messing it up, but I don't feel like a fake *person* around them. I'm still their daughter. We still do family dinners on Sundays, and I know they love me and I belong there. 

So, yeah, it's really just when I put on my steel-toe boots and walk onto the actual job site. That’s when it hits me. It's like the second I step out of my truck and see the crew and the blueprints, I just get this overwhelming, crushing sense that I don't belong there and I'm fooling everyone. But outside of that? With my friends and family and stuff? No, I don't really have that feeling at all.
When you're not at work—like when you're with your friends at the diner or at home with your family—do you still feel down, sad, or hopeless most of the time?

Well, um, yeah, I do. Actually, I really do. It's not just a work thing, the feeling down part, I mean. Like, even when I'm at the diner with my friends, which used to be my favorite part of the week... I'll just be sitting there in our usual booth, and they'll be laughing about something, maybe recounting a story from high school or talking about a movie they saw, and I just... I can't really connect to it. I'm there, physically, but mentally I'm just so bogged down. It's like this heavy blanket is over me all the time. I try to smile and nod along so I don't ruin the vibe, because I don't want to be the one bringing everyone down, you know? But inside, I just feel this deep, lingering sadness that won't lift, no matter how hard I try to just enjoy my fries and be present. 

And it's the same at home. Sunday dinners with my parents used to be so nice, but lately, I just sit at the table pushing my food around. My mom will ask me how things are going, or my dad will make a joke, and I just feel so hollow. I don't feel that spark of joy I used to get from just being around them. It's like I'm just going through the motions of my life. I'll go to my room after dinner and just sit on my bed, staring at the wall, feeling completely hopeless about everything. Like, what's the point? It doesn't matter if I'm at work, or with my friends, or safe in my own house... that sad, empty feeling just follows me everywhere. It's exhausting, honestly. Just constantly feeling like I'm dragging myself through every single day, even the parts that are supposed to be the good parts.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things that used to make you happy, like hanging out at the diner with your friends or spending time with your family?

Yeah, exactly. It's exactly that. I mean, I know I was just saying how the diner feels empty and Sunday dinners feel hollow, but it’s honestly bleeding into literally every single other part of my life, too. It’s not just the social stuff with my friends and family. It’s the things I used to do just for me, the hobbies I used to absolutely love. 

Like, I’ve always been really into drawing. I have this specific sketchbook—it’s this really nice, heavy-duty one with thick paper that my mom got me for my birthday a couple of years ago—and I used to take it everywhere. I’d sketch out pipe layouts for practice, or just draw people when I was sitting at a coffee shop, and it was so relaxing. But lately? It just sits right on the corner of my desk. I can walk past my sketchbook every single day, multiple times a day, and I don't even feel a tiny urge to pick up a pencil. It’s just collecting dust, and I don't even care. 

And it’s the same thing with my volleyball league. I play in this rec league on Tuesday nights at the community center, and I used to look forward to it all week long. I’m usually the setter, so I’m really involved in the plays, getting everybody hyped up and moving around. But for the past few weeks, I’ve just been skipping it. I’ll just text the captain and make up some excuse about being too exhausted from the job site, which is a lie, I just... I can't bring myself to go. And the craziest part is that I don't even feel bad about missing it. 

I’m doing it with my volunteer group, too. We do these weekend park cleanups and we have this massive, super active group chat. My phone will just be buzzing and buzzing with all these texts from them planning the next meetup or sending pictures, and I just swipe the notifications away. I just ignore the volunteer group texts completely without feeling much of anything. No guilt, no FOMO, nothing. It’s honestly kind of scary when I stop and think about it, because drawing, playing volleyball, volunteering... those used to be the things that made me feel like myself. They were my identity outside of being an apprentice. And now it’s like someone just flipped a switch and I couldn't care less about any of it.
Over the past two weeks, have you noticed that you have little energy or feel fatigued almost every day, even when you haven’t done anything physically or mentally taxing?

Um, no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, I definitely get tired, but it’s not for no reason. My job is just so incredibly physical, you know? Like, as an apprentice, I’m the one doing a lot of the heavy lifting. I’m lugging around these massive lengths of steel pipe, and I’m constantly kneeling on hard concrete, twisting these huge pipe wrenches that weigh a ton all day long. So by the time I clock out and climb into my truck, yeah, my arms feel like jelly and my back is usually aching. But that’s a completely normal kind of tired. That’s just from busting my butt on a job site for eight or ten hours. 

But if I haven’t done anything? Like on a Saturday when I’m just hanging around the house? No, I don’t feel physically fatigued at all. My body actually feels totally fine. I don't have that heavy, weak feeling in my muscles or anything. Like, I have the physical energy to get up and do things. I could physically go for a run or clean my whole room if I wanted to. It’s just... I just don't *want* to, because of that whole mental block, that sadness I was telling you about. It’s not that my body is out of energy, it’s just that my mind doesn't see the point in using it. 

I actually remember when I had a really bad case of the flu back in high school, and *that* was real fatigue. Like, I literally couldn't even walk from my bedroom to the kitchen to get a glass of water without needing to sit down on the hallway floor to catch my breath. It was awful. But what I'm feeling right now isn't like that at all. My physical energy levels are completely normal as long as I haven't been hauling cast iron around all day. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel fatigued when I haven't been doing anything physically taxing. It's really just the mental stuff.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently, like eating a lot more or a lot less than usual?

Um, no, not really. I mean, my appetite hasn't changed at all, honestly. I know a lot of people, when they get into a slump or feel sad like this, they either completely stop eating and lose a ton of weight, or they go the total opposite direction and just sit around binge-eating junk food all day. But for me, it’s just been exactly the same as always. 

I still eat my normal three meals a day. Like, every morning before I head out to the job site, I still make my usual two scrambled eggs and a couple pieces of toast, because if I don't eat a solid breakfast, I'll literally be shaking by 10 AM trying to hold a heavy wrench, you know? You just can't do this kind of physical labor on an empty stomach. And for lunch, I pack the exact same thing I always do—usually a turkey and provolone sandwich, an apple, and a bag of pretzels. I just sit on my cooler at the site and eat it like I always have. 

And even when I was talking about the diner earlier, or Sunday dinners at my parents' house... like, I might be pushing my food around the plate for a minute because I'm feeling so disconnected from the conversation, but I still end up eating all of it. I still order my usual bacon cheeseburger and fries with my friends, and I finish the whole basket. It just doesn't bring me the same joy it used to, but the physical hunger is definitely still there. 

So I haven't lost any weight or gained any weight, either. My work jeans fit exactly the same as they did six months ago, and my tool belt sits on the exact same notch it’s been on since I started this apprenticeship. So, yeah, no changes there at all. My body still demands the exact same amount of fuel for the work I do, even if my brain is completely checked out, if that makes sense. I haven't had to buy new clothes or anything. It's just completely status quo when it comes to food and my weight.
Have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, even when there’s no specific reason for it?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I know I used the word 'sadness' a minute ago when we were talking about my energy levels, but... it’s not like I’m walking around with this heavy, dark cloud over my head all day, every day. It's not like I'm actively depressed or sitting around crying for no reason. It's really different from that. 

Like, when I'm at the job site, my brain is just totally dialed into the work. If I'm helping my journeyman rough-in a commercial bathroom or something, I have to be completely focused. I'm measuring out lengths of pipe, checking the pitch on the lines, making sure every single fitting is perfectly to code... because, you know, if you mess up the slope on a drain line, it's a massive, expensive disaster for everybody later on. So I'm doing all this math in my head, coordinating with the other trades, dodging the electricians and the drywall guys, and during all of that? I'm not feeling down at all. I'm just... working. I feel completely normal. I'll joke around with the guys on my crew during our coffee break, complain about the general contractor, all that totally normal stuff. I don't feel like crying or feeling miserable while I'm doing it. 

So, no, it’s not an all-day depression kind of thing. It's really just that weird emptiness I mentioned earlier when it comes to the fun stuff—my sketchbook, the diner, volleyball. But as far as just feeling depressed all day for no reason? No, definitely not. I get up, I lace up my steel-toes, I go do my job, and I feel fine emotionally while I'm doing it. It's just a blankness when I clock out, not an actual depressed feeling, if that makes sense.
Have you noticed that you have trouble concentrating, making decisions, or thinking clearly lately, even when you’re trying your best to focus?

Um, no, definitely not. My focus is actually completely fine. I mean, I really have to be sharp every single day on the job, right? Like I was saying a minute ago about roughing-in those commercial bathrooms, there is just zero room for error when you're dealing with plumbing systems. Just yesterday, for example, my journeyman handed me this massive set of blueprints for the second-floor water supply lines, and I had to sit there and calculate all the offsets for the copper piping because we had to route it around this huge HVAC duct that the tin knockers decided to install right where our main run was supposed to go. You know how it is on a site, the trades are constantly stepping on each other's toes and you just have to adapt. So I had to figure out the exact angles, do all the math in my head for the cut lengths, take into account the fitting allowances for the elbows, and then actually prep and solder the whole assembly together. And I did it perfectly on the first try, no leaks at all during the pressure test. If my brain was foggy or I couldn't concentrate, there is no way I could pull that off. 

And as for making decisions, that's totally normal too. You're constantly making split-second calls when you're pipefitting. Like, if a supplier shorts us on two-inch PVC, I have to figure out on the fly if we can adapt what we have with different fittings or if I need to jump in the truck and make a run to the supply house, and I don't hesitate at all. My brain feels totally clear. Even when I'm doing something super tedious, like threading black iron pipe for gas lines—which takes a ton of attention to detail so you don't strip the threads or get the cutting oil all over the floor—I'm completely dialed in. I don't lose my place, I don't forget what I'm doing halfway through a task, none of that. 

So, yeah, my concentration is honestly one hundred percent. If I couldn't focus or think clearly, I'd probably end up flooding an entire floor of a building or messing up a gas line, and my boss would have fired me months ago. My mind is sharp as a tack. Like I said before, it's really just that weird blankness when I get home and try to do my hobbies or hang out, but the actual thinking, focusing, and deciding part of my brain? That's completely normal.
Have you ever felt this way before, like you’re going through the motions and nothing brings you joy, or is this the first time you’ve experienced these feelings?

Um, well, as for if I've felt this way before... I mean, this specific feeling, this whole stretch of just going through the motions, it’s actually been with me for a while now. It's not like it just popped up yesterday or even last month. I've been thinking about it, and this depressed stretch has actually been with me for about nine months now. 

At first, you know, I tried to just brush it off. I figured, oh, I'm just tired from lugging cast iron all day, or maybe I'm just getting bored of my usual routine, so I'd just force myself to smile at the diner with my friends, or I'd force myself to go to volleyball even if I didn't want to, just to pretend everything was normal. I thought I was doing a pretty good job of faking it, honestly. But it became harder to hide once school and work started slipping. 

And, I mean, when I say slipping, I don't mean my actual pipefitting—like I said a minute ago, my measurements and my actual physical work on the site are still dead-on, because they have to be. But my overall presence, I guess? Like, I'm doing my associate's degree classes at night for the apprenticeship program, right? Blueprint reading, advanced hydraulics, building codes, all that stuff. And I used to be the one in the front row, raising my hand, asking the instructor a million questions, really getting into the theory behind why we pipe things a certain way. But over these last nine months, that just completely faded out. I started just sitting in the back of the classroom, staring at the whiteboard, just totally checked out and not participating at all. 

And at work, even though my welds are fine, my journeyman definitely started noticing something was off. He started asking if I was getting enough sleep, or if I was mad at him, because I wasn't jumping into the banter in the morning, or I'd take a little longer to drag myself out of the truck when we got to the site. It just started taking so much energy to put on the mask and act like I cared about the day. So, yeah, it's been about nine months of this. It’s just been this long, slow drag where keeping up appearances at the job site and at night school just got heavier and heavier to maintain, so people definitely started to see the cracks, even if I was trying my hardest to keep it all under wraps.
Over the past two weeks, have you found yourself having trouble thinking clearly, making decisions, or focusing on tasks nearly every day?

Wait, didn't we just go over this a second ago? I feel like I just answered this, but... no, even if we're just looking at the past two weeks specifically, my focus is still completely fine. Like I was saying before, I really haven't had any trouble at all with thinking clearly or making decisions. 

I mean, just to give you another example from literally last week—we were doing this massive commercial water heater installation, right? It was this huge 119-gallon gas-fired unit for a restaurant downtown. You have to be so dialed in for those. I was the one handling the venting, measuring out the B-vent piping, and I had to make sure the clearance to combustibles was exactly, perfectly to code because the inspector in that specific county is notoriously strict. Like, he will literally fail your entire inspection if you're off by a quarter of an inch, and then the restaurant can't open on time, and it's this whole huge disaster. So I was doing all the math for the BTUs, double-checking that our gas line was sized right—we were running one-inch black iron for the main branch and then dropping down to three-quarter for the actual connection to the unit. I had to dope and tape every single joint, wrench it all down tight, and then do a soap test on every connection to check for leaks. 

If my head was cloudy over these last two weeks, or if I couldn't make a decision, I’d just be standing there staring at my pipe wrenches like an idiot while my journeyman yelled at me to hurry up. But I didn't. I knocked the whole thing out, no leaks, passed inspection on the first try. So, yeah, I don't know if maybe I didn't explain it right the first time, but my thinking is honestly crystal clear. I'm making decisions just fine, whether it's picking the exact right fittings off the truck or figuring out how to route a drain line around a floor joist without losing my pitch. There's no fog, no confusion, nothing like that at all. It's really just that weird lack of interest in my fun stuff that I mentioned, but my actual brain power? Totally normal.
Have you had periods in the past where you felt this way—like you're going through the motions and nothing brings you joy—for more than two weeks at a time?

Wait, I... I feel like we're going in circles here a little bit. Didn't I just mention this a few minutes ago? Like, when you asked if I'd felt this way before? But, um, to answer your question about the two weeks... yes, way more than two weeks. Like I was trying to explain earlier, this whole depressed stretch, this feeling of just going through the motions and not caring about my hobbies or hanging out, it has been with me for about nine months now. It's been one continuous thing. It's not like I had two weeks of it, and then I was fine, and then it came back. It's just been this long, unbroken nine-month stretch. 

I remember when it first started, I really thought it was just a phase, you know? Like maybe I just needed a vacation or something, or maybe I was just burnt out from the overtime. Because for the first few months, I was actually hiding it really well. I'd still go to the diner with my friends, I'd still show up to volleyball and pretend to care if we won or lost, even though inside I was just completely empty and counting down the minutes until I could go home and just stare at the wall. 

But yeah, it definitely became way harder to hide once school and work started slipping. Because you can fake a smile at a diner, right? You can just nod and laugh when someone tells a joke. But you can't fake the energy it takes to actively participate in a three-hour night class on advanced hydraulics or building codes after you've been on a freezing job site since six in the morning. Like I was saying before, I went from being the girl in the front row asking all the questions to just... a ghost in the back row. And at work, when my journeyman started noticing I was dragging my feet and taking forever to get out of the truck in the mornings... that's when it really hit me that I couldn't keep the mask on anymore. The weight of pretending for nine whole months just got too heavy. So, yeah, definitely way, way more than two weeks.
Have you had multiple separate periods in your life where you felt this same kind of emotional emptiness or loss of interest, or has this been the only time you’ve felt this way?

Um, no, it's really just been this one time. Like, just this continuous nine-month stretch we've been talking about. I haven't had, like, different separate blocks of it over the years or anything like that. 

Before this started... I mean, I've always been a super high-energy person. Like, back in high school, and even when I first started my apprenticeship right after graduation, I never had anything like this happen. I was always the girl who would wake up at 4:30 in the morning, lace up my steel-toed boots, pack my cooler, work a full ten-hour shift hauling cast iron or threading steel pipe, and then I'd still have the energy to go play in a weekend-long volleyball tournament or hang out at the diner with my friends until closing. I just didn't stop. 

I never even had, like... a phase where I was just empty or checked out. You know how some people get like that in high school? Like that whole teenage angst thing where everything is suddenly boring and they just want to sleep all day and they hate the world? I never did that. I was always go-go-go, always wanting to learn the next thing, always wanting to get my hands dirty on the job site and prove I could keep up with the older guys. 

So when this started nine months ago, it was completely out of left field for me. I kept waiting for it to just pass, because I figured, hey, I've never felt like this before, it's gotta just be a weird fluke, right? Like maybe I just caught a bug or the winter weather was getting to me. But it didn't pass. It just stayed, and it got heavier. But yeah, to answer your question, before this past nine months? Never. Not once. I've never had a period where I felt this checked out or lost interest in my life before. This is definitely the first and only time it's ever hit me like this, which is honestly probably why it took me so long to even realize what was happening. I just had absolutely no frame of reference for it, you know? Because I've just never been this kind of person before.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this nine-month stretch where you felt down, lost interest in things, or felt emotionally empty for more than two weeks at a time?

Wait, I'm sorry, are you asking something different this time? Because I really feel like I just answered this exact thing a second ago. Did I not explain it right? 

But, um, just to be absolutely, one hundred percent clear... no. No, never. Not for two weeks, not for two days, not ever. Before these last nine months, I have never felt down or empty or lost interest in my life. 

Like I was trying to say about my baseline before all this started... I was literally the opposite of depressed. I was the person annoying everyone else on the crew with how awake I was at 5 AM. I remember when I was 18, right out of my associate's program, I got put on this massive commercial rough-in for a new medical building. We were hauling four-inch cast iron pipe up three flights of stairs because the service elevator wasn't certified yet. It was just backbreaking, miserable work. You're sweating through your high-vis shirt by 7 AM, your shoulders are screaming, and you're covered in dirt and flux. And even then, I wasn't down. I wasn't empty. I was cracking jokes, I was racing the other apprentices to see who could prep the no-hub couplings faster, I was completely engaged. 

If I had been depressed or empty back then, like for two whole weeks? There is no way I would have survived that job site. The journeymen would have eaten me alive if I was just moping around or staring into space. In this trade, especially being a young woman, you have to have thick skin and high energy. You have to constantly prove you want to be there and that you can pull your weight. And I *did* want to be there. I loved it. I loved the exhaustion at the end of the day because it felt earned, you know? I'd go home, shower off the grime, and still want to go out and do things. 

So, yeah, I really don't know how else to say it, but no. I never had any two-week periods of feeling like this before. It is literally just this one, single, incredibly long nine-month stretch that I'm in right now. That's it.
Have you ever had a period in your life before this nine-month stretch where you felt down, lost interest in things, or felt emotionally empty for more than two weeks at a time?

Okay, wait, seriously, is there a glitch in the matrix right now? Because I feel like I am losing my mind a little bit. You... you literally just asked me that. Like, I think word for word, you just asked me that exact same question. Is this like a memory test or something? Or are you trying to see if my story changes if you ask it enough times? Because I promise you, I'm not hiding anything from you, and my answer isn't going to change. 

But, um, I guess I'll just say it again... no. No, I have never, ever had a period in my life before this nine-month stretch where I felt down or empty for two weeks. 

I don't know if I'm just not explaining my past well enough, or if you're looking for a specific answer that I'm just not giving you, but I really need you to understand that this is entirely new for me. Like I was saying about the job sites and being the most awake person on the crew at 5 AM... that wasn't an act. That was just who I was. Even when I was younger, like in middle school and high school, I never had that moody, lock-myself-in-my-room phase that a lot of kids get. My mom used to joke that I was the easiest teenager on the planet because I was always just out in the garage helping my dad fix up old dirt bikes, or I was studying for my apprenticeship entrance exams, or I was at volleyball practice. I didn't have time to be down. I didn't *want* to be down. 

So, yeah, before these last nine months? I never lost interest in things. Not for two weeks, not ever. I loved my life. I loved my job, I loved threading pipe and getting my hands dirty, I loved hanging out at the diner. This nine-month stretch is the very first time my brain has ever done this to me, and it's the only time I've ever felt this emotionally blank. So... no. Never before this. I really, really hope that makes sense this time, because I honestly don't know how else to describe it to you.
Have you ever had any episodes of feeling down or losing interest in things before this nine-month period, even if they were brief?

Okay, I... I really don't mean to be rude or anything, but are you guys like, recording this for a study? Because I swear this is the fourth time we are going over the exact same thing. You're just adding the word "brief" to it now. 

But... okay, to answer the "brief" part. No. Still no. I mean, look, everybody has a bad day, right? If I'm crammed under a vanity trying to sweat a copper joint in some nasty, spider-infested crawlspace and I drop my torch, or if the general contractor is breathing down my neck about a deadline when our supply house hasn't even delivered the PVC yet—yeah, I get ticked off. I might be grumpy for an afternoon. But that's just being frustrated with work. That's not... this. That's not feeling down or losing interest in my life. 

Even when things actually sucked, like... okay, when I first tried for my braze certification and I messed up the nitrogen purge, so the inside of the pipe oxidized and I failed. I was so mad at myself. I went home, threw my boots at the wall, and was just totally sour for the rest of the evening. But by the time my alarm went off the next morning? I was already over it. I was back in the shop before anyone else, practicing on scrap pieces because I wanted to nail it the next time. I didn't lose interest in pipefitting. I didn't feel empty or hollowed out. I was just fired up to fix my mistake. 

So, no. Not for two weeks, not for two days, not even for a brief little blip. Before this whole nine-month nightmare started, my brain just didn't do the whole shutting-down thing. I was always fully dialed in to whatever I was doing. I really, really hope that covers it this time, because I feel like I'm beating a dead horse here and I don't know how many other ways I can say that I was just a completely normal, happy, energetic person before all this. Can we please talk about something else now?

latest_inference.note: The patient has experienced a single, continuous episode of depression lasting over nine months without any prior episodes, ruling out recurrent depression codes with multiple episodes (F33.2). Additionally, the patient does not meet criteria for a current major depressive episode (F32.2, F32.3) due to absence of symptoms such as depressed mood most of the day, fatigue, concentration difficulties, or changes in appetite. The absence of prior episodes confirms the diagnosis as persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) F33.3.

doctor.intent: Identify the patient's chief complaint or reason for seeking help
doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: What made me come in is that I keep feeling like I ruined things for everybody, like I'm a fake in the apprenticeship and I let my family and the younger apprentices down over stuff I know other people would probably just fix and move on from.

patient.answer:
Hi. Yeah, thank you. Um, so, honestly, it's just been a lot lately, and I guess that's what made me finally come in. I just... I keep having these overwhelming feelings that I've completely ruined things for everybody around me. 

I'm in an apprenticeship right now—I'm a pipefitter and plumber—and I got my associate's degree before this, so my parents and everyone made this really huge deal about me getting into the trades and getting a good union spot. But lately, I just feel like a complete and total fake. Like I'm totally tricking the journeymen into thinking I know what I'm doing, when I don't. And it's just this incredibly heavy feeling, you know? I look at my family, who brag about me all the time to their friends, and I just feel like I'm letting them down so badly by being an imposter. And even at work, there are these younger apprentices who just started their first year, and they kind of look to me to know what's going on because I've been there a little longer, and I just feel like I'm failing them too. I'm supposed to be setting a good example and I'm just not.

And the most frustrating part is that I'm feeling this way over stuff that really shouldn't be a big deal. Like, minor mistakes on a job site. I know for a fact that if anyone else on the crew made the same mistake—like mismeasuring something by a fraction of an inch or taking a little too long to thread a pipe—they would just fix it, grab a new piece of material, and move right on with their day like nothing happened. It's just part of the job. But for me, I just dwell on it. I can't let it go. I feel like this massive burden on the whole crew, like I'm dragging the entire project down and ruining the day because I'm a fraud. I just can't seem to shake this awful guilt that I'm messing everything up for everyone.

Um, no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, I definitely get tired, but it’s not for no reason. My job is just so incredibly physical, you know? Like, as an apprentice, I’m the one doing a lot of the heavy lifting. I’m lugging around these massive lengths of steel pipe, and I’m constantly kneeling on hard concrete, twisting these huge pipe wrenches that weigh a ton all day long. So by the time I clock out and climb into my truck, yeah, my arms feel like jelly and my back is usually aching. But that’s a completely normal kind of tired. That’s just from busting my butt on a job site for eight or ten hours. 

But if I haven’t done anything? Like on a Saturday when I’m just hanging around the house? No, I don’t feel physically fatigued at all. My body actually feels totally fine. I don't have that heavy, weak feeling in my muscles or anything. Like, I have the physical energy to get up and do things. I could physically go for a run or clean my whole room if I wanted to. It’s just... I just don't *want* to, because of that whole mental block, that sadness I was telling you about. It’s not that my body is out of energy, it’s just that my mind doesn't see the point in using it. 

I actually remember when I had a really bad case of the flu back in high school, and *that* was real fatigue. Like, I literally couldn't even walk from my bedroom to the kitchen to get a glass of water without needing to sit down on the hallway floor to catch my breath. It was awful. But what I'm feeling right now isn't like that at all. My physical energy levels are completely normal as long as I haven't been hauling cast iron around all day. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel fatigued when I haven't been doing anything physically taxing. It's really just the mental stuff.

I know a lot of people, when they get into a slump or feel sad like this, they either completely stop eating and lose a ton of weight, or they go the total opposite direction and just sit around binge-eating junk food all day. But for me, it’s just been exactly the same as always. 

I still eat my normal three meals a day. Like, every morning before I head out to the job site, I still make my usual two scrambled eggs and a couple pieces of toast, because if I don't eat a solid breakfast, I'll literally be shaking by 10 AM trying to hold a heavy wrench, you know? You just can't do this kind of physical labor on an empty stomach. And for lunch, I pack the exact same thing I always do—usually a turkey and provolone sandwich, an apple, and a bag of pretzels. I just sit on my cooler at the site and eat it like I always have. 

And even when I was talking about the diner earlier, or Sunday dinners at my parents' house... like, I might be pushing my food around the plate for a minute because I'm feeling so disconnected from the conversation, but I still end up eating all of it. I still order my usual bacon cheeseburger and fries with my friends, and I finish the whole basket. It just doesn't bring me the same joy it used to, but the physical hunger is definitely still there. 

So I haven't lost any weight or gained any weight, either. My work jeans fit exactly the same as they did six months ago, and my tool belt sits on the exact same notch it’s been on since I started this apprenticeship. So, yeah, no changes there at all. My body still demands the exact same amount of fuel for the work I do, even if my brain is completely checked out, if that makes sense. I haven't had to buy new clothes or anything. But as far as just feeling depressed all day for no reason? No, definitely not. I get up, I lace up my steel-toes, I go do my job, and I feel fine emotionally while I'm doing it. I remember when it first started, I really thought it was just a phase, you know? Like maybe I just needed a vacation or something, or maybe I was just burnt out from the overtime. I'd still go to the diner with my friends, I'd still show up to volleyball and pretend to care if we won or lost, even though inside I was just completely empty and counting down the minutes until I could go home and just stare at the wall. 

But yeah, it definitely became way harder to hide once school and work started slipping. Because you can fake a smile at a diner, right? You can just nod and laugh when someone tells a joke. But you can't fake the energy it takes to actively participate in a three-hour night class on advanced hydraulics or building codes after you've been on a freezing job site since six in the morning. Like I was saying before, I went from being the girl in the front row asking all the questions to just... a ghost in the back row. And at work, when my journeyman started noticing I was dragging my feet and taking forever to get out of the truck in the mornings... that's when it really hit me that I couldn't keep the mask on anymore. The weight of pretending for nine whole months just got too heavy. So, yeah, definitely way, way more than two weeks.

patient.answer:
Um, no, it's really just been this one time. Like, just this continuous nine-month stretch we've been talking about. I haven't had, like, different separate blocks of it over the years or anything like that. 

Before this started... I mean, I've always been a super high-energy person. Like, back in high school, and even when I first started my apprenticeship right after graduation, I never had anything like this happen. I was always the girl who would wake up at 4:30 in the morning, lace up my steel-toed boots, pack my cooler, work a full ten-hour shift hauling cast iron or threading steel pipe, and then I'd still have the energy to go play in a weekend-long volleyball tournament or hang out at the diner with my friends until closing. I just didn't stop. 

I never even had, like... a phase where I was just empty or checked out. You know how some people get like that in high school? Like that whole teenage angst thing where everything is suddenly boring and they just want to sleep all day and they hate the world? I never did that. I was always go-go-go, always wanting to learn the next thing, always wanting to get my hands dirty on the job site and prove I could keep up with the older guys. 

So when this started nine months ago, it was completely out of left field for me. I kept waiting for it to just pass, because I figured, hey, I've never felt like this before, it's gotta just be a weird fluke, right? Like maybe I just caught a bug or the winter weather was getting to me. But it didn't pass. It just stayed, and it got heavier. But yeah, to answer your question, before this past nine months? Never. Not once. I've never had a period where I felt this checked out or lost interest in my life before. This is definitely the first and only time it's ever hit me like this, which is honestly probably why it took me so long to even realize what was happening. I just had absolutely no frame of reference for it, you know? Because I've just never been this kind of person before.

patient.answer:
Wait, I'm sorry, are you asking something different this time? Because I really feel like I just answered this exact thing a second ago. Did I not explain it right? 

But, um, just to be absolutely, one hundred percent clear... no. No, never. Not for two weeks, not for two days, not ever. Before these last nine months, I have never felt down or empty or lost interest in my life. 

Like I was trying to say about my baseline before all this started... I was literally the opposite of depressed. I was the person annoying everyone else on the crew with how awake I was at 5 AM. I remember when I was 18, right out of my associate's program, I got put on this massive commercial rough-in for a new medical building. We were hauling four-inch cast iron pipe up three flights of stairs because the service elevator wasn't certified yet. It was just backbreaking, miserable work. You're sweating through your high-vis shirt by 7 AM, your shoulders are screaming, and you're covered in dirt and flux. And even then, I wasn't down. I wasn't empty. I was cracking jokes, I was racing the other apprentices to see who could prep the no-hub couplings faster, I was completely engaged. 

If I had been depressed or empty back then, like for two whole weeks? There is no way I would have survived that job site. The journeymen would have eaten me alive if I was just moping around or staring into space. In this trade, especially being a young woman, you have to have thick skin and high energy. You have to constantly prove you want to be there and that you can pull your weight. And I *did* want to be there. I loved it. I loved the exhaustion at the end of the day because it felt earned, you know? I'd go home, shower off the grime, and still want to go out and do things. 

So, yeah, I really don't know how else to say it, but no. I never had any two-week periods of feeling like this before. It is literally just this one, single, incredibly long nine-month stretch that I'm in right now. That's it.
